column1: # ---- 04-compliance/T6 ----
T0 through T5 test the engine against inputs it is supposed to handle, while T6 tests it against inputs designed to break a specific claim.
The claims T6 attacks are the ones that, if false, invalidate everything else.
The claim that the engine cannot use information it did not have is attacked by lookahead poisoning.
The claim that unknown configuration is rejected rather than ignored is attacked by config poisoning.
The claim that a malformed payload is rejected cleanly and never partially read is attacked by contract fuzzing.
The claim that the commitment ledger is authoritative and tamper-evident is attacked by ledger tampering.
The claim that a stale artefact is refused rather than used silently is attacked by the stale-artefact audit.
Each attacked claim is one the architecture makes in prose, and T6 is where the prose is turned into an executable attack.
The lookahead poisoning audit runs a backtest with all facts having knowledgeTime greater than t replaced by garbage and asserts bit-identical results, and if any component peeks the run diverges.
The lookahead poisoning audit is the single most decisive test in the specification.
The poisoned and reference runs must agree on the whole-run golden hash and on every per-tick golden record.
On a poisoning failure the Merkle chain names the first artefact that diverged, which names the layer that peeked.
The PoisonedStore wraps the Belief store and, for every read, replaces the value of any row whose knowledgeTime exceeds the tick's asOf before the row can reach anything.
The poison is applied at the storage layer below the asOf filter, so a correctly-implemented engine never observes it and a peeking one gets nothing usable.

The Garbage poison mode replaces future rows with deterministic pseudo-random values drawn from the series' own plausible range, seeded from the manifest, and catches a component that uses the future quantitatively.

The NaN poison mode replaces every numeric field of a future row with NaN and catches a component that reads the future at all, because NaN either changes the output or trips the no-NaN invariant, both of which are detections.
The NaN mode is the loudest and the first to run.

The Shuffled poison mode permutes the true future values across valid_time within the series, preserving every marginal moment and destroying every temporal alignment, and catches a component that uses only distributional properties of the future.
The Constant poison mode replaces future rows with a single fixed value, catching a component whose use of the future is masked by averaging, and serving as a control.
A run that is bit-identical under all four poison modes is strong evidence of no leak.

Shuffled is the mode most likely to find a real defect in a codebase that has already fixed the obvious leaks, because a future variance or future range used to size a bound is easy to introduce accidentally and impossible to see in review.
The lookahead audit is only meaningful because runs are deterministic, since otherwise a changed result proves nothing.
The lookahead audit is a null test whose assertion is that two runs are identical, and its entire inferential content lies in identity being achievable at all.

Without determinism, two runs would differ by some amount even with no poisoning, because of thread-scheduling-dependent floating-point reduction order, a wall-clock time limit, or hash-order iteration.

Without determinism the audit would have to ask whether the observed difference exceeds a noise floor, which requires estimating that floor, which requires many runs, turning a decisive test into a statistical one.
A component that peeks slightly, using the future to nudge a bound by 0.3 per cent, produces a difference smaller than the noise floor and is undetectable without determinism.
The failure mode the bitemporal store exists to prevent is a backtest that looks like alpha, which is precisely a small, systematic, hard-to-see improvement.
With determinism the assertion is hash equality and any leak of any size anywhere in the pipeline produces a hash difference the Merkle chain localises to a single artefact in a single tick.
Determinism turns the lookahead test from statistically inconclusive to decisive and self-diagnosing.
The cheap, decisive lookahead audit is purchased by the determinism discipline and is the largest single return that discipline pays.

The poisoning scope covers every source of future information, not just prices: the day-ahead and intraday price series, the spread belief, the aFRR capacity and energy prices, activation, imbalance price, load, pv, meter data, settlement revisions, cleared day-ahead, reserve awards and fill outcomes.
The poisoning scope also covers every model artefact fitted on data after the tick.
The negative control injects a deliberate leak — reading load a day ahead to set the safety margin — and asserts the audit fails and the localisation names the expected artefact and tick.
The negative control runs in the same job, because an audit that has never been observed to fail is an audit nobody knows is wired up.
The lookahead audit is easy to break silently, because a PoisonedStore that is constructed but not installed passes perfectly.
The full audit says whether something peeked while the partial variant says what, by poisoning one series at a time and reporting which series' future values affect the run.
The partial-poison variant costs one backtest per series, which is affordable on the canonical window, and is run on demand after a full-audit failure rather than nightly.

The lookahead audit runs nightly on the canonical window in the NaN and Garbage modes, pre-release on full history in all four modes plus the negative control, and on full history in all four modes blocking after any change to L1 or the Belief store.
A lookahead divergence is a stop-ship rather than a bug to be triaged.
Every backtest result produced since the last clean lookahead audit is suspect, and the release does not proceed until the leak is found and the audit is clean on the full history.
Each remaining T6 section defends a specific claim that other levels assume.
The closed tariff component list is enforced so that an unrecognised component is a configuration error rather than a silently ignored field.
Every numeric tariff threshold is configuration and never a constant.
The configuration failure mode is specific and expensive: a typo'd key is silently dropped, the default applies, and the engine runs a configuration nobody intended while every test passes.
Unknown configuration keys are rejected rather than ignored, and the error names the key and suggests the nearest valid key.
A valid configuration key with an out-of-range value is rejected at load rather than at use.
A valid configuration key with the wrong type is rejected and never coerced.
A tariff component outside the closed enumeration is rejected.
A required configuration key that is absent is rejected, with no silent default for anything that has no conservative default.
In layered configuration an override file with an unknown key fails the same way as the base.
The resolved configuration is what is hashed into the manifest, and two different layerings producing the same resolved config produce the same config hash.

If the manifest hashed the config files rather than the resolved result, two runs with different layering but identical effective settings would appear different, and a change that alters resolution without altering any file would appear identical.
Materially changing a regulatory threshold must change the run's golden hash, so a threshold that has silently become a hardcoded constant is detected.
Consumer-side validation failure is a HALT because a contract violation means the producer is in an unknown state and nothing downstream can be trusted.
The dangerous outcome of a malformed payload is not a crash but a consumer that read the first eight fields, acted on them, and then rejected the ninth.
Only two outcomes are permitted for a fuzzed payload: accepted, or rejected with an invariant id; never a crash, hang, partial accept or silent truncation.
Rejection is atomic: the consumer state is unchanged, the invariant id is one of the declared families, the message names the field and the violated range, and nothing is emitted downstream.
Acceptance of a fuzzed payload implies all invariants hold on it.
Numeric mutations — NaN, positive and negative infinity, negative zero, denormals and the maximum double — must be rejected by the no-NaN or range invariants.
A range mutation placed in the middle of an array is the mutation that catches a validator checking only the first element.
Length mutations — an array one element short, one long, or empty — must be rejected by the horizon-length invariants.
A scenario-indexed array with a different scenario count must be rejected by the shared-axis invariants.
Weights summing to one within only 1e-3, or a negative weight, must be rejected by the weights invariant.
An unknown major version, an unknown minor version, or a missing schemaVersion must be rejected by the version invariant.
A corrupted contentHash or an empty inputHashes must be rejected by the hashing invariant.
An absent non-nullable field must be rejected by the nullability invariants.
An out-of-range EconomicEffect, VarSymbol, BoundReason or DegradationMode must be rejected by the symbol and bound-reason invariants.

Structural mutations — a duplicate termId, a PwlTerm with non-increasing X, a mis-declared curvature, or a FillProbView term carrying a price — must be rejected by the curvature and fill-probability invariants.
Encoding mutations — truncated binary, trailing bytes, deeply nested JSON, a 100 MB string field — must produce a clean rejection with bounded memory and no hang.
Adversarial encodings — duplicate JSON keys, integer overflow in a length prefix, a self-referential inputHashes — must produce a clean rejection.
Cross-field mutations — socMin above socMax, a round-trip efficiency above one, or a blockIndex not covering every slot — must be rejected by the corresponding belief invariants.
The fuzzer is structure-aware rather than byte-random, because random bytes are rejected by the deserialiser and test nothing above it.
The fuzzer mutates valid payloads at the field level, which is where the interesting failures are.
The fuzz seed corpus is the recorded seams of the designated audit days, so mutations start from realistic structure.
A payload that crashes rather than rejecting is minimised and added to the permanent conformance corpus in the same commit as the fix.
Each fuzz iteration runs under a memory and time cap, and a payload that causes unbounded allocation is a finding rather than a timeout to be raised.

The commitment ledger is the one piece of state where a corruption is both plausible, because it is written by two producers, and expensive, because an undetected loss of a confirmed award produces exactly the delivery shortfall treated as a prequalification risk.
Deleting a Confirmed reserve award that C4 reported must be detected by the award-coverage invariant and halt.
Flipping a Confirmed ledger entry to Cancelled must be detected by the award-coverage invariant and the award/ledger reconciliation, and halt.
Flipping a Pending ledger entry to Confirmed must be detected by reconciliation against C4, because no fill or award backs it, and halt.

Promoting a pending entry to confirmed is the dangerous direction, because the Planner would treat phantom exposure as a hard constraint and over-constrain itself, or worse, believe a position it does not hold.
Stripping the feasibilityRequirement from a Confirmed reserve award must halt, because without the corridor the Planner cannot see the obligation.
Widening a feasibilityRequirement corridor so the obligation looks easier must be caught by a cross-check against the product's sustain duration and the prequalification requirement, and halt.
Altering the signed volume on a settled ledger entry must be caught by the no-backward-write invariant and halt.
Altering the signed volume on a Confirmed ledger entry must be caught by reconciliation against C4 fills and halt.
Introducing a fill with no matching intent must be caught as a phantom fill and halt.
Duplicating a ledger entry must be rejected by idempotency on the entry id rather than double-counted.
Reordering ledger entries must leave the tick's output unchanged, because the ledger is keyed and ordered.

Replaying a stale ledger from a previous tick must be caught by the no-backward-write invariant and by the assertion that the tick's state snapshot hash equals the previous tick's state update hash, and halt.
Corrupting the ledger's own content hash must be caught by the hashing invariant and halt.
On a ledger tampering detection the engine goes to HALT rather than continuing with a reduced obligation, an alert is raised, and operator acknowledgement is required.
The ledger's content hash is recorded in the StateSnapshot and a restart from that snapshot reproduces the identical ledger.
A tampering attack that survives a restart, because the ledger was rebuilt from a source other than the snapshot, breaks the claim that L0 is the entire state.

The stale-artefact failure is the quietest in the system: a value function fitted three weeks ago on a different peak state still evaluates, still returns plausible euros, still produces a feasible plan, and prices the entire end of the horizon wrongly.
Within the validity horizon the mode stays NORMAL and the value function's slopes are unshrunk.

Beyond the validity horizon the mode is at least DEFENSIVE, the slopes are shrunk by the staleness penalty, the driver summary names the stale value function, the tier escalates, and a refresh is requested.
The validity boundary is not silently crossed and the transition at the horizon is observable in the artefact record.
The engine must never be beyond the validity horizon while in NORMAL mode with unshrunk slopes.

The tempting stale-artefact implementation logs a warning and proceeds, which is the silent-imputation failure applied to a model artefact: the engine makes full-confidence decisions on a stale value function and the failure is invisible until Settlement.
Every artefact in the manifest declares a validity policy, and an artefact with no declared policy fails the audit by construction.
A scenario ensemble or reduction is stale by its generation asOf versus the tick asOf and by its horizon versus H_plan, and an ensemble not covering the horizon is Missing rather than truncated.
The fill model halts on a simulator version mismatch and alerts on age.
The activation model alerts on fit date and realised calibration drift and widens the chance level in response.
The Tier-3 surface is stale by fit date and by out-of-training-envelope detection on the current state, and the response is escalation to Tier 2, logged and visible in the settlement record.
The MarketCalendar is checked for coverage of the tick's slot and the whole accounting period, and a tick outside calendar coverage is a HALT because it cannot be priced.
tzdata must be present and matching the manifest, and is a HALT if absent or mismatched.

Peak and qualification state staleness is signalled by the unsettled gap and the provisional flag, and the response is to treat the gap conservatively using the engine's own modelled trajectory rather than assuming the gap contained nothing.
A model artefact fitted on data later than the backtest position is a lookahead leak the PoisonedStore cannot see, because the leak is baked into the artefact rather than read from the store.

Every model artefact's training data end must not exceed the run's first tick asOf, and for a rolling refit the artefact in force at a tick must have a training data end at or before that tick's asOf.
An artefact with no declared training data end cannot be used in a backtest, and every artefact declares one.
Artefact temporal hygiene is a separate audit from lookahead poisoning and is the one people forget.
A Tier-3 surface fitted on the whole history and then backtested over that same history will show an excellent gap and will not reproduce live.
The holdout discipline in the gap gate depends on the artefact temporal hygiene check being real.
Lookahead poisoning in the NaN and Garbage modes runs nightly on the canonical window and pre-release on full history, and failure is a stop-ship.
Lookahead poisoning in the Shuffled and Constant modes runs pre-release on full history, and failure is a stop-ship.
The negative control runs on every pre-release run, and its failure is a stop-ship because the audit is not wired up.
Partial-poison localisation runs on demand and on failure.
Config poisoning runs in full nightly and pre-release, and failure blocks release.
Contract fuzzing runs 10^5 iterations nightly and 10^7 pre-release, and any crash, hang or partial read blocks release.
Ledger tampering runs in full nightly and pre-release, and failure blocks release.
The stale-artefact audit runs in full nightly and pre-release, and failure blocks release.
Artefact temporal hygiene runs in full nightly and pre-release, and failure is a stop-ship of the same class as a lookahead leak.
A T6 report accompanies every release and records, for each audit, the corpus, the manifest, the number of iterations and the negative control's result.
An audit that passed without its negative control passing is reported as not run.

A lookahead or temporal-hygiene failure invalidates history: every backtest result, every gap report and every calibration report produced since the last clean audit is suspect and is marked as such in the archive.
A lookahead failure is not proportionate-response territory, because a lookahead leak produces results that look like alpha so the results cannot be trusted merely because they look reasonable.

A fuzzing crash is a HALT that did not happen: the consumer was supposed to reject and instead did something else, so it is treated as a contract defect, the validator is fixed, and the payload is added to the conformance corpus.
A ledger-tampering miss is a delivery risk, sitting upstream of the delivery shortfall invariant, which is a prequalification risk rather than an accounting item.
A stale-artefact miss is a slow leak that costs money quietly and shows up months later as a rising unexplained ratio, by which point the attribution is gone.
